What the official sources say

  • Security deposit limit: one month's rent for an unfurnished unit; 1.5 months if furnished; plus up to 1/2 month's rent extra if pets are allowed. (K.S.A. 58-2550(a); source)
  • Landlord may enter at reasonable hours after reasonable notice to inspect, repair or show the unit to purchasers; no fixed number of hours stated; entry without consent allowed for extreme hazard. (K.S.A. 58-2557; source)
  • Landlord may not retaliate by raising rent or decreasing services after the tenant complains to a code agency or the landlord, or joins a tenants' union; tenant has a defense to possession actions. (K.S.A. 58-2572(a),(b); source)

Which Kansas laws govern landlords and tenants?

Most residential rentals in Kansas fall under the Kansas Residential Landlord and Tenant Act, K.S.A. 58-2540 through 58-2573. Mobile home parks have their own act, and rentals of non-residential property are covered by K.S.A. 58-2501 through 58-2533.

The Legislative Research Department points out one carve-out in K.S.A. 58-2573. The residential act does not protect a person who enters and stays in a dwelling without a rental agreement and without the landlord's knowledge, knowing they have no right to be there, after the landlord has personally told them to leave. A tenant under a rental agreement, written or not, falls on the protected side of that line.

Kansas Legal Services makes a point that surprises many owners: when the lease is silent, the statute fills the gaps. So a seller who inherits a rental with no lease on file is still bound by the act's notice, deposit and repair rules.

What are the main Kansas tenant rights at a glance?

TopicKansas ruleAuthority
Security deposit, unfurnishedUp to one month's rentK.S.A. 58-2550
Security deposit, furnishedUp to 1.5 months' rentK.S.A. 58-2550
Pet depositUp to half a month's rent extraK.S.A. 58-2550
Deposit return14 days after deductions are set, 30 days at mostK.S.A. 58-2550
Wrongful withholdingDamages of 1.5 times the amount withheldK.S.A. 58-2550
Month-to-month ending30 days, on a rent-paying dateK.S.A. 58-2570
Week-to-week ending7 daysK.S.A. 58-2570
Landlord entryReasonable hours, reasonable noticeK.S.A. 58-2557

The figures come from the cited statutes and the Kansas Legal Services tenant guide, which also notes that a federal rule bars an extra deposit for a certified service or assistance animal.

What does a Kansas landlord owe the tenant during the tenancy?

A Kansas landlord must keep the rental fit to live in, and the tenant must keep paying rent regardless. Kansas Legal Services explains that the two duties are separate, so a tenant who withholds rent over repair problems can still be taken to court for nonpayment.

Under K.S.A. 58-2553, the landlord has to comply with building and housing codes that affect health and safety. The landlord also has to keep electrical, plumbing, sanitary, heating and air-conditioning equipment that the landlord supplies in good working order, and has to supply running water, reasonable hot water and heat.

When repairs are ignored, the tenant has two documented options:

  • Give written notice of at least 30 days ending on a rent-paying date. The landlord then has 14 days to begin repairs, or the lease ends on the date named.
  • Sue to force repairs and recover damages, including rent paid for a place that was not livable.

Kansas Legal Services recommends calling the local housing or code office before choosing either route. A tenant may also make repairs under a separate written agreement with the landlord, and the cost can then come off the next rent payment, though work required by building codes should be done by the landlord.

A seller who knows a rental has open repair issues should expect those complaints to follow the property into a sale.

When can a landlord enter a rented Kansas house?

A landlord may enter at reasonable hours after reasonable notice to inspect, make repairs or show the unit to purchasers. K.S.A. 58-2557 sets no fixed number of hours, though Kansas Legal Services says 24 hours is common.

Entry without consent is allowed in an extreme hazard. This matters directly to owners who are selling, because showings are the most frequent reason for entry. Written notice with a proposed time leaves a clear record of what was asked.

The statute also bars retaliation. Under K.S.A. 58-2572, a landlord may not raise rent or reduce services because the tenant complained to a code agency or to the landlord, or joined a tenants' union, and the tenant has a defense in a possession action. A sale-driven eviction that follows soon after a repair complaint can invite that defense.

What happens to a tenant's rights when the landlord sells?

A sale does not cancel the tenancy by itself, but it does shift who answers for what. K.S.A. 58-2554 says a landlord who conveys the premises in a good-faith sale to a bona fide purchaser is relieved of liability under the rental agreement and the act for events after written notice of the conveyance goes to the tenant. The former landlord remains liable for any deposit amount the tenant is entitled to.

The statute begins with the words unless otherwise agreed, so the sale contract can allocate the deposit differently between buyer and seller. Ask the closing agent to say plainly in the file who holds the deposit.

Owners preparing to sell a rental usually do the following:

  • Pull the lease, the move-in inspection list and the deposit record.
  • Send the tenant the written notice of the conveyance, and keep a dated copy.
  • Check whether any repair requests are outstanding.
  • Decide whether the buyer is taking the house with the tenant or vacant.

We buy houses as-is and can work with an occupied rental. Tell us what the lease says and what condition the house is in, and we will explain what a sale could look like.

How does a Kansas lease end?

A lease ends by its own terms, by proper notice, or through eviction. Kansas Legal Services notes that a landlord usually must give at least 30 days' notice that it will not renew, and that many leases ask the tenant for more, sometimes 60 days.

A tenancy does not always end when the lease term does. If the landlord takes the next month's rent, a month-to-month tenancy often follows. If the landlord does not take it, the landlord can serve a three-day notice to leave. A tenant who moves out without telling the landlord may owe another month.

Security deposits come with specific mechanics. The tenant has to move out entirely, tell the landlord, return the keys and make a written demand. Kansas Legal Services also says a landlord who keeps part of the deposit should send an itemized list within 30 days of move-out, and that a tenant generally cannot use the deposit as last month's rent unless the landlord agrees.

Which special situations change the rules?

Three situations come up often enough that sellers should know them.

  • Military orders: A service member with permanent change of station orders, a deployment order or a call to support an operation lasting at least 90 days can end a lease. The tenancy ends 30 days after the day rent is next due, or with 15 days' notice on a month-to-month tenancy.
  • Natural disaster: If fire, flood or tornado makes the home unlivable, the tenant does not have to stay and can end the lease with written notice.
  • Disability and fair housing: The federal Fair Housing Act bars discrimination in renting and selling housing on the basis of race, gender, religion, familial status, disability or ethnicity, and landlords must allow reasonable accommodations. A landlord may still consider criminal history, credit and financial stability.

If you are selling, fair housing rules apply to how you treat the tenant and any buyer.

Rent paid by mail counts as paid when it is properly sent, according to Kansas Legal Services, which is why tenants are told to keep dated proof.

More questions about Kansas Landlord Tenant Law and Tenant Rights

How much can a Kansas landlord charge for a security deposit?

Up to one month's rent for an unfurnished unit and 1.5 months for a furnished one, plus up to half a month's rent more if pets are allowed, under K.S.A. 58-2550.

How long does a Kansas landlord have to return a deposit?

14 days after determining deductions, and no more than 30 days after the tenancy ends, possession is delivered and the tenant demands it. Wrongful withholding carries damages of 1.5 times the amount withheld.

What happens to the tenant if the landlord sells the house?

The tenancy continues. The landlord is relieved of later liability once written notice of the sale goes to the tenant, but still owes any deposit the tenant is entitled to.

Can a Kansas landlord show a rental to buyers?

Yes, at reasonable hours and after reasonable notice under K.S.A. 58-2557. There is no fixed hours figure in the statute.

How much notice ends a month-to-month tenancy in Kansas?

Written notice of at least 30 days, ending on a rent-paying date, from either side. Week-to-week tenancies need 7 days.

What the official sources say

  • Holdover tenant: landlord may bring an action for possession; willful holdover can recover up to 1.5 months' rent or 1.5 times actual damages. (K.S.A. 58-2570(c); source)
  • Removal is by the person named in the writ of restitution (anyone authorized to serve process), executed within 14 days, reasonable force allowed. (K.S.A. 61-3808; source)

Which notice does a Kansas landlord have to give first?

It depends on why the landlord wants the tenant out. The Kansas Residential Landlord and Tenant Act sets different written notices for unpaid rent, for a lease violation and for ending a periodic tenancy, and each one has its own wording requirements.

SituationNotice periodStatute
Unpaid rent3 days (three consecutive 24 hour periods)K.S.A. 58-2564(b)
Material lease violationTermination at least 30 days after receipt if not fixed within 14 daysK.S.A. 58-2564(a)
Repeat of a similar breach30 days, with no chance to cureK.S.A. 58-2564(a)
Month-to-month tenancy30 days, ending on a rent-paying dateK.S.A. 58-2570(b)
Week-to-week tenancy7 days before the termination dateK.S.A. 58-2570(a)

All of these notices are in writing. The text of each section is on the Kansas Legislature's site, for example K.S.A. 58-2564.

How are the three days for unpaid rent counted in Kansas?

The clock starts when the notice is delivered or posted, and it runs as three full 24 hour periods. K.S.A. 58-2564(b) says that if the notice is served on the tenant or on a person over 12 years of age living on the premises, or posted in a conspicuous place on the premises, the period begins at delivery or posting.

If the notice goes by mail, the statute allows an additional two days from the date of mailing. The notice must state that rent is unpaid and that the landlord intends to end the rental agreement if it is not paid within the three days. Read the statute before drafting, because those two statements are part of what the notice has to say.

If the tenant pays the full rent within the period, the termination does not take effect. A landlord who is unsure how the notice was served should keep a record of the date, the time and the method used, since the three days are counted from that moment.

What about a lease violation or an expired lease?

For a material breach, the landlord delivers a notice that lists the acts or omissions and says the agreement will end on a date at least 30 days after receipt if the breach is not remedied in 14 days. If the problem can be fixed by repairs or payment and the tenant makes a good faith effort before the date in the notice, the agreement does not terminate.

When the same or a similar breach recurs after the 14 days, the landlord may serve a new 30 day notice that gives no chance to cure. The agreement then ends as the notice says, regardless of the periodic rent-paying date.

A tenant who stays after the lease term ends, or after termination, without the landlord's consent is a holdover. Under K.S.A. 58-2570(c) the landlord may bring an action for possession. If the holdover is willful and not in good faith, the landlord may recover up to 1.5 months' periodic rent or up to 1.5 times actual damages, whichever is greater. A tenant in the military who needs to end a month-to-month tenancy because of orders needs to give no more than 15 days' written notice.

What happens in court after the notice period ends?

The landlord files an eviction petition, and K.S.A. 61-3801 through 61-3808 govern those lawsuits. The Kansas Judicial Branch's self-help site gives a typical timeline of up to 42 days from petition to the end of the process.

  • Step 1: the landlord files a petition. The hearing is scheduled within 3 to 14 days.
  • Step 2: the court issues a summons. The tenant must respond in writing or appear at the hearing, or a default judgment can be entered.
  • Step 3: if the tenant responds and disagrees, a bench trial is set within 14 days of the hearing date.
  • Step 4: the judge rules.
  • Step 5: if the landlord wins, a writ of restitution issues and is executed within 14 days.

Service of the summons in a forcible detainer case must be returned no later than three days before the date set for the tenant to appear or plead (K.S.A. 61-3005). The Kansas Judicial Council posts forms and instructions for both landlords and tenants.

Who can carry out the eviction in Kansas?

Only the person named in the writ of restitution, who must be someone authorized to serve process. The statute names no other route for removal after judgment.

K.S.A. 61-3808 says the writ must be executed within 14 days after the named person receives it, and that person may use reasonable force as needed. If the tenant appeals and the court stays the proceedings, the officer must stop at once, and if the tenant has already been removed, the tenant is restored to the home.

There is also a faster option in some cases. K.S.A. 58-2570(d) lets a landlord ask for an order of immediate possession during an action for possession. The judge must be satisfied that it is in the interest of justice, and can require the landlord to post an undertaking to cover the tenant's damages if the tenant wins.

What new Kansas eviction record rules apply in 2026?

Starting July 1, 2026, some eviction cases in Kansas can be expunged, which removes the court record from public view. The Kansas Judicial Branch runs an online Eviction Expungement Portal for people who represent themselves, and the change comes from 2026 Substitute for House Bill 2357.

For a landlord, this means a former tenant may later ask a court to expunge a case, and the landlord may object using the form provided. For a seller, it is a reason to keep copies of the notice, the petition and any judgment in your own files, since the public record may not always be there to prove what happened.

How does an eviction affect selling a Kansas rental house?

A house with a tenant in a dispute is harder to sell on the open market, because buyers who plan to live in it expect possession at closing. The notices above only work if they are accurate, delivered correctly and followed by the court steps, which can take up to 42 days even when nothing goes wrong.

Some counties run programs that can help both sides settle first. The Kansas self-help site lists the Johnson County District Court's Eviction Mediation Program, the Douglas County Eviction Resolution Program and the Sedgwick County Eviction Resolution Program, which connect landlords and tenants with information, mediation and rental assistance.

  • Kansas Legal Services publishes a Landlord Handbook and a tenant rights guide.
  • The Kansas Housing Resource Corporation and 211 Kansas list rental help and emergency shelter.
  • Ask a Kansas attorney whether an existing lease continues after a sale of the house, since the answer depends on the lease terms.

More questions about Kansas Eviction Notice Rules

How many days notice is required to evict for nonpayment in Kansas?

Three days, counted as three consecutive 24 hour periods after delivery or posting, with two extra days if the notice is mailed (K.S.A. 58-2564(b)).

How much notice ends a month-to-month tenancy in Kansas?

At least 30 days after receipt, ending on a rent-paying date. A tenant in the military with orders can give no more than 15 days (K.S.A. 58-2570(b)).

How long does a Kansas eviction take after the notice?

The Kansas Judicial Branch says the court process can take up to 42 days. A hearing is set 3 to 14 days after the petition, and a writ must be executed within 14 days.

Can a landlord remove a tenant without a court order?

No. Removal is done by the person named in the writ of restitution, under K.S.A. 61-3808, after a judgment for possession.

Can an eviction case be removed from the record in Kansas?

Starting July 1, 2026, some eviction cases can be expunged through a court motion. The Judicial Branch offers an online portal for self-represented people.
